National Register of Historic Places listings in Buffalo, New York

stops.name: Buffalo City Hall
stops.description: A 398-foot Art Deco slab finished in 1931, still the seat of city government, with a 28th-floor observation deck open free on weekdays for the best view of Lake Erie in the city.

stops.name: McKinley Monument
stops.description: The 96-foot marble obelisk at the center of Niagara Square, guarded by four sleeping lions, marks the assassination of President William McKinley at Buffalo's 1901 Pan-American Exposition.

stops.name: St. Paul's Episcopal Cathedral
stops.description: Richard Upjohn considered this 1851 sandstone Gothic Revival church his finest work, and it is one of only a handful of churches in the country designated a National Historic Landmark.

stops.name: Guaranty Building
stops.description: Louis Sullivan's 1896 terra-cotta tower is the textbook example of the early American skyscraper, its entire skin covered in swirling ornament that reads like embroidery from the sidewalk.

stops.name: Ellicott Square Building
stops.description: When it opened in 1896 this Burnham-designed block was the largest office building in the world, and its glass-roofed marble atrium is still open to walk through.

stops.name: Old Post Office
stops.description: A Gothic Revival pile of granite finished in 1901 that sorted Buffalo's mail until 1963 and has housed SUNY Erie's city campus since 1981, with a soaring skylit interior court.

stops.name: Soldiers and Sailors Monument
stops.description: An 85-foot granite shaft in the middle of Lafayette Square, ringed by bronze figures for the infantry, artillery, cavalry and navy, carrying half of the Gettysburg Address carved into its base.

stops.name: Hotel Lafayette
stops.description: This French Renaissance hotel was designed by Louise Blanchard Bethune, the first woman admitted to the American Institute of Architects, and reopened in 2012 after a 35 million dollar restoration.

stops.name: Liberty Building
stops.description: Two 36-foot replicas of the Statue of Liberty stand on the roof of this 1925 tower, one facing east and one west to mark Buffalo's place between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic.

stops.name: Buffalo Savings Bank
stops.description: The gilded dome on this 1901 bank is 56 feet across and has been releafed three times, most recently with 140,000 sheets of 23.75-carat gold.

stops.name: Electric Tower
stops.description: Built in 1912 as a monument to Niagara hydropower, this white terra-cotta tower is floodlit in seasonal colors and hosts Buffalo's New Year's Eve ball drop.

stops.name: Shea's Buffalo Theatre
stops.description: A 1926 movie palace by Rapp and Rapp with Tiffany-designed interiors, saved from demolition by volunteers and still running touring Broadway shows.

stops.name: Buffalo and Erie County Naval & Military Park
stops.description: The largest inland naval park in the country, where you can board the cruiser USS Little Rock, the destroyer USS The Sullivans and the submarine USS Croaker, all moored at Canalside.

stops.name: Michigan Street Baptist Church
stops.description: Built in 1845 by Buffalo's Black community, this brick church sheltered freedom seekers on the last leg to Canada and anchors the Michigan Street African American Heritage Corridor.

stops.name: Colored Musicians Club
stops.description: Founded in 1935 by members of Buffalo's segregated Black musicians' union, this upstairs room hosted Armstrong, Ellington and Fitzgerald and still runs jam sessions above its ground-floor jazz museum.

note: Buffalo, NY - first run for this city; it had never appeared in the nightly.json history (9 prior runs: Cleveland, Denver, Boston, Dallas, Detroit, Green Bay, Houston, Atlanta, Baltimore), so it wins outright. 15 stops verified article by article. All 15 have a street address and a looked-up ZIP; none are missing one. The cluster is the Main Street spine from Canalside north to the Theatre District, with a western arm to Niagara Square and an eastern arm to the Michigan Street African American Heritage Corridor - about a 1.5 mile loop, slightly over the 1 mile target because the two heritage-corridor stops sit roughly half a mile east of Main. Drop either if you want it tighter. DELIBERATE OMISSIONS: (1) Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site, 641 Delaware Ave, 14202 - the room where TR took the oath in 1901 and arguably the single best stop in Buffalo, but it is a mile north of Niagara Square and would have roughly doubled the loop. Verified and ready if you want it. (2) Old County Hall, 92 Franklin St, 14202 - a fine 1875 granite courthouse with a 270-foot clock tower, dropped only to avoid a third stop on Niagara Square. (3) Erie County Savings Bank, which the GeoSearch returns but which was demolished in 1968. Also skipped: Metro Rail stations, hospitals, and the several NRHP-listed apartment blocks and factories that carry an address but nothing worth standing in front of. Guaranty Building address is 140 Pearl St per the building's own tenants; the NRHP row files it as 28 Church St, same corner. Old County Hall is 92 Franklin per the Erie County Clerk, though the Wikipedia article says 100 Franklin.
